sources.title: What is the difference between a nautical mile and a knot?
sources.summary: - The international nautical mile is exactly 1.852 kilometres.

Publisher: NOAA National Ocean Service

Source: https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/nautical-mile-knot.html

Retrieved: 2026-10-01T00:49:02.552182+00:00

## Original research notes

- The international nautical mile is exactly 1.852 kilometres.
- A knot expresses speed in nautical miles per hour, rather than distance.

## Application and limits

The physics conversion is 1852/3600 metres per second per knot. This unit reference does not validate vessel resistance or sail coefficients.

These are original notes. Source rights remain with the publisher; the complete webpage is not redistributed here.

sources.title: UK International Certificate for Operators of Pleasure Craft
sources.summary: RYA explains the UK ICC as evidence of competence under UNECE Resolution No. 40 and describes its authority to issue it for the UK government. Categories concern vessel type and coastal and/or inland waters; they are not a universal Basic/Intermediate/Advanced ladder. Eligibility, evidence and acceptance depend on the issuing process and applicable flag/coastal-state legislation. A shorebased certificate alone does not establish every vessel category. The primary UNECE endpoints returned HTTP 403 during this research, so this is a verified issuing-authority explanation, not a direct verification of the resolution text.

sources.title: Bareboat Cruising Certification Standards

sources.title: Basic Cruising Certification Standards
sources.summary: This standard follows Basic Keelboat and covers an auxiliary-powered cruising yacht by daylight within sight of land in moderate conditions. It adds vessel systems inspections, crew briefing, VHF, navigation and local regulations; power handling includes windage, prop walk, spring lines and controlled arrivals. It also requires sail controls, reefing, rescue, anchoring and emergency responses. Published practical outcomes explicitly include stopping, tying up and securing the boat.

## Original summary

This standard follows Basic Keelboat and covers an auxiliary-powered cruising yacht by daylight within sight of land in moderate conditions. It adds vessel systems inspections, crew briefing, VHF, navigation and local regulations; power handling includes windage, prop walk, spring lines and controlled arrivals. It also requires sail controls, reefing, rescue, anchoring and emergency responses. Published practical outcomes explicitly include stopping, tying up and securing the boat.

- Include crew capabilities and emergency preparation in passage decisions.

## Application and limits

Use sail-33–34 early and revisit in Advanced. The app should never issue an offshore-survival credential or count button presses as physical rescue.
